fixes.explanation: True, baker. David's message says, “Ask your young men, and they will tell you.” He's inviting Nabal to check the story with his own people. He points Nabal to his own workers for the answer.
It's actually true. David's message says, “Ask your young men, and they will tell you.” He points Nabal to his own workers to confirm it. The invitation is right there in the message.

Shearers is it. Nabal says, “Why should I take my bread and water and the meat I have slaughtered for my shearers, and give them to these men whose origin I do not know?” He says he doesn't know these men's origin, and that's the question he asks about giving them anything.
Close to home, but no. Nabal says he slaughtered the meat “…for my shearers…” Those are the men who work his flocks. The word he uses is shearers, not family.
Sickness isn't the word, friend. The young man says, “…disaster looms over our master and all his household.” He wants Abigail to think carefully about what she must do.

Proud is a fair guess for a man who snaps at messengers, but it's not the meaning Abigail gives. She says, “His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.” She says it to David as she asks him to pay Nabal no attention.

Hunger isn't it, friend, even though Abigail did show up with a big load of supplies. She says the LORD “…has held you back from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand…” The word is bloodshed, not hunger.

David already has men following him, but that's not the promise. Abigail says, “…the LORD will surely make a lasting dynasty for my lord, because he fights the LORD’s battles.” The promise is a dynasty, baker, not an army.
True, baker. Abigail says that when the LORD has done all the good He promised, “…He has appointed you ruler over Israel…” She says it to David face to face. That's a big thing to hear in a ravine.
She never asks him to leave. Her last words are, “And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant.” Her request is to be remembered, not to see him go anywhere.
No payment, friend. She's giving the gift freely, and her last request is, “And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, may you remember your servant.” What she asks for is to be remembered.

Samuel is a good guess, but he had already died at the start of this chapter. David blesses “…the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day!” The blessing goes to the LORD, not to a prophet.
Saul, Israel's king, isn't part of this meeting at all, friend. David says, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me this day!” The blessing goes to the LORD.
Yes. David says, “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request.” He receives what she brought and sends her off in peace. That's his answer after hearing her out.
He doesn't invite her along. He says, “Go home in peace. See, I have heeded your voice and granted your request.” He sends her home, baker, not off to Carmel with his men.

True, baker. Abigail finds Nabal in high spirits and very drunk, so she tells him nothing until morning light. She tells him in the morning, when he's sober. That's the day after a feast fit for a king.
That's it. When Nabal hears, “…his heart failed within him, and he became like a stone.” It's a heavy moment, so I'll say it plainly. I think this one hurts.
Moving away isn't what the text says. It says that about ten days later, “…the LORD struck Nabal dead.” It's a heavy line, baker.
No famine here, friend. David says, “…the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” The thing brought down on Nabal is his own wickedness.
David's sword isn't what the text names, friend. He says, “…the LORD has brought the wickedness of Nabal down upon his own head.” He also thanks the LORD for restraining him from evil.
She did give good advice, friend. But David's message asks her to become his wife. So the word is wife, not advisor.
Ally is a fair guess after that meeting in the ravine. But David asks her to become his wife. So the word is wife, not ally.
The text shows the opposite, friend. Abigail “…hurried and got on a donkey…” She follows David's messengers with five of her maidens. No taking her time here.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “David had also married Ahinoam of Jezreel. So she and Abigail were both his wives.” Abigail isn't the only one, and the next verse calls Michal David's wife too.
True, friend. Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim. That's the closing verse of the chapter. It still calls Michal David's wife.
It's true, baker. Saul had given his daughter Michal, David's wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim. That's how the chapter closes. The text still calls Michal David's wife there.
